title: Weak Bones (Osteoporosis): Signs, Tests, Treatment and Preventing Fractures
metaDescription: Osteoporosis often has no symptoms until a bone breaks. Learn the risk factors, the bone density scan, treatment choices and ways to lower fracture risk.
intro: Osteoporosis means the bones have become weak and break more easily. It often causes no symptoms, and the first sign is frequently a broken bone after a minor fall. A bone density scan can check bone strength, medicines can help keep bones stronger for longer, and exercise and fall prevention lower the chance of a fracture.

sections.heading: What is osteoporosis?
sections.body: Osteoporosis literally means spongy bone. Bone density falls and the inner structure weakens, so bones break more easily. Some bone loss with age is normal, and the word is used only when bones become quite fragile. Bone loss usually starts around age 40, and women are about four times more likely than men to develop it, mainly because bone loss speeds up after menopause.

sections.heading: What are the signs of weak bones?
sections.body: Often there are none. It develops slowly over several years. A fracture after a minor fall or knock, most often in the hip, spine or wrist, can be the first sign. Small fractures in the spine can cause the changes below. Back pain that has not improved after a few weeks needs a doctor's visit.
bullets: A curved spine or hunched posture

sections.heading: Who is more likely to get osteoporosis?
sections.body: Risk rises with age and after menopause. Other risk factors include a parent with osteoporosis, low calcium or vitamin D intake, being underweight, smoking, heavy alcohol use and low physical activity. Conditions such as diabetes or rheumatoid arthritis, and taking steroid tablets for a long time, also raise the risk.

sections.heading: How is osteoporosis tested?
sections.body: Your doctor assesses your risk, asks about symptoms and may examine you. They may refer you for a DEXA scan (a bone density scan). It takes about 15 minutes and uses a very small amount of X-ray. Routine scanning of everyone is not recommended. It is advised for people with a fracture from a minor fall, long-term steroid use, early menopause, a parent with a hip fracture or certain other conditions.

sections.heading: How is osteoporosis treated?
sections.body: Medicines can help keep bones stronger for longer. Bisphosphonates slow bone breakdown and are taken as tablets, liquid or injection. They usually take 6 to 12 months to work, and treatment may last 5 years or longer. Other medicines are used when these do not suit you or the condition is severe. Each has possible side effects, so the choice depends on your scan results, age and sex and is made with your doctor. Calcium and vitamin D are often prescribed alongside.

sections.heading: How can I lower my chance of a fracture?
sections.body: Daily habits make a difference, and care is tailored to you. Useful steps are:
bullets: Regular weight-bearing exercise such as walking, plus strength and balance exercises. T'ai Chi can improve balance and lower fall risk.
Foods rich in calcium, and a vitamin D supplement if advised
Not smoking, and keeping alcohol within 14 units a week
Reducing fall risks at home, for example with grippy shoes and non-slip bath mats

sections.heading: What if a bone has already broken?
sections.body: Fractures are treated first, usually with a cast, manipulation or surgery, plus pain relief. Our usual approach is to settle pain with medicines, then restore movement and strength. Surgery is offered only where it is appropriate. We explain the options and the patient decides. Treating the weak bones themselves then helps lower the risk of the next fracture. Medicines for osteoporosis are taken for years, so we also review how you are getting on.

faqs.q: How long do osteoporosis medicines take to work?
faqs.a: Bisphosphonates usually take 6 to 12 months to work. Treatment is long term. Your doctor will review it over time, and bone density scans may be repeated every 2 to 5 years.

faqs.q: Is exercise safe with weak bones?
faqs.a: Weight-bearing activity such as walking is helpful. High-impact exercise may not suit people who already have osteoporosis, so check with a doctor or physiotherapist first.

faqs.q: Do calcium and vitamin D alone fix osteoporosis?
faqs.a: No. They are often prescribed alongside other treatment. Ask your doctor whether you need them and how much.
